extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, instrument-makers, navigators, and readers of the Philosophical Transactions (late 17th-century scientists and educated practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, constructing, and standardizing thermometers (choice of fluid, graduation points, and experimental method) based on Halley's experiments and recommendations. The page also contains related natural-history observations and a separate curriculum-like list for a treatise of navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities measured by effect on magnitude or motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities, such as heat and cold, moisture and dryness, and the like, are not otherwise to be estimated, but by their effect on the magnitude of some body they act on, by increasing or lessening its dimensions: or else by the motions they produce; both which subject them to mensuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use change in dimensions (expansion/contraction) or produced motions as the basis for measuring qualities like heat and cold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different fluids expand differently — fluids must be chosen carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: For the same degree of heat does not proportionally expand all fluids; some swelling with a gentle warmth, and others not till they be considerably hot; ... so that no one of them increases and diminishes in the same proportion with the heat, and consequently, that the thermometers graduated by equal parts of the expansion of any fluid, are not sufficient standards of heat or cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume any single fluid gives a linear/proportional scale across temperatures; test fluids across the intended range and note their non-uniform expansion behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water is an improper fluid for thermometers in northern climates
rubrics_metrics.description: Water, increasing so very little with all the degrees of heat the air receives from the sun, was a very improper fluid to make a thermometer of; and, besides, any freezing liquor is useless for this purpose in these northern climates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid water for sealed thermometers in climates where freezing is possible and because water's expansion is small and non-sensitive to gentle warmth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercury as a thermometer fluid — sensitivity and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: This fluid being so sensible of a gentle warmth, and also not subject to evaporate without a good degree of fire, might most properly be applied to the construction of thermometers, were its expansion more considerable. ... I observed that 125 ounces of mercury had increased by the space of 810 grains, or a 74th part of its bulk when cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mercury responds noticeably even to gentle warmth and resists evaporation, but its absolute expansion is small; account for this when designing graduations. Also note mercury's thermal expansion will slightly affect barometer readings (seasonal bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit of wine as thermometer fluid — large expansion but volatile and variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of wine... at the point of boiling, it had increased a 12th part in bulk: which great dilatation makes it a liquor sufficiently adapted to our purpose, were it not for its evaporation, and for the difference in the goodness of the spirit; and because that in length of time it becomes as it were effete, and loses gradually a part of its expansive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spirit of wine gives large expansion useful for sensitivity and as an upper reference (boiling point), but requires highly rectified/dephlegmated spirits to reduce variability and suffers from evaporation and ageing; account for these when selecting and maintaining fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air as the properest fluid for thermometers
rubrics_metrics.description: I find that the heat of summer expands the ordinary air about a 30th part; ... we may conclude ... which is as great an expansion as that of spirit of wine when it begins to boil; for which reason, and for its being so very sensible of warmth or cold, and continuing to exert the same elastic power, after being ever so long included, in my opinion it is the properest fluid for the purpose of thermometers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Air shows large, persistent, and relatively consistent expansion across seasons and does not suffer the evaporation/degeneration issues of spirits; thus it is recommended as the working fluid for reliable thermometry, pending precise calibration of its expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method for measuring expansion (bolt-head and neck method)
rubrics_metrics.description: I took a large bolt-head, holding about 3½ lb. of water, with a narrow neck, to show the increase more sensible; ... noted exactly to what mark the water rose; then immersed it into a skillet of warm water ... In other trials I used a smaller bolt-head with mercury and spirits of wine, marking ascensions and subsidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a large bulb with a narrow neck, mark fluid heights before and after heating by immersion/boiling, and measure retained expansion after cooling to quantify volumetric dilation. Repeat and compare across fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical expansion findings as calibration guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured results: water — to reach the boiling-rise mark required an additional 1/26 of the bulk; mercury — 125 ounces increased by 810 grains (≈1/74); spirit of wine — increased ≈1/12 at boiling; air — summer expansion ≈1/30, extreme cold contraction ≈1/20 (Boyle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical magnitudes as illustrative benchmarks when selecting and comparing fluids; expect water to expand very little, mercury modestly, spirits substantially at boiling, and air to show large seasonal variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermometer graduation: use stable, well-determinable reference points
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual thermometers with spirit of wine do some of them begin their degrees from a point which is that where the spirit stands when it is so cold as to freeze oil of aniseeds; and others from the point of beginning to freeze water; I conceive these points are not so justly determinable, but with a considerable latitude: and that the just beginning of the scales of heat and cold should not be from such a point as freezes any thing, but rather from temperature, such as is in places deep under ground; where the heat of the summer, or cold in winter, have been found to have no manner of effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing graduation on freezing points of variable substances; instead choose reproducible and stable fixed points — e.g., deep-underground constant temperature or well-defined boiling or evaporation phenomena — and calibrate other marks relative to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use boiling point of rectified spirits as an upper scale limit and fix other fluids accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: This degree of heat, which caused spirits of wine to begin to boil, being determined so nicely, made me conclude, that this might very properly be taken for the limit of the scale of heat in a thermometer; and its effect in the expansion of any other fluid being accurately noted, might be easily transferred to any sort of thermometer whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a reproducible boiling/boiling-onset point (from carefully rectified spirit) as an upper calibration anchor, and measure expansions of other fluids relative to it to create comparable scales across instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for accurate experiments on air expansion before final recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: I thought to have finished this discourse with showing a method of constructing and regulating thermometers to the best advantage; but finding it necessary to make some experiments with more accuracy than I have yet done, especially on the air's expansions, I crave leave... to inform myself more fully in the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform precise and repeated measurements of air expansion under controlled conditions before finalizing graduation methods and recommended fluids; avoid premature standard-setting without sufficient data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that spirit used for boiling-point reference be highly rectified/dephlegmated
rubrics_metrics.description: Only it must be observed, that the spirit of wine used to this purpose, be highly rectified or dephlegmated; for otherwise the different goodness of the spirit will occasion it to boil sooner or later, and so prevent the designed exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chemically consistent, highly purified spirits to ensure reproducible boiling behavior; variability in spirit quality undermines calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: evaporative losses and dew condensation in sealed thermometers
rubrics_metrics.description: During this experiment it appeared, both by the dew on the neck, and by the scent in the room, that though the neck was about 30 inches long, yet the spirits evaporated very fast, considering the smallness of the surface of the liquor. And I have often noted the like evaporations condensed in dew within the head of the ordinary sealed thermometers, in very hot weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for evaporation and internal condensation when using volatile fluids; sealed designs must be checked for internal condensation and long-term stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for determining value of lives from mortality tables (use of logarithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Were the calculus from the bills of mortality founded on the experience of a very great number of years, it would be worth while to think of methods for facilitating the computation of the value of two, three, or more lives... all that can be done to expedite it is, by tables of logarithms ready computed, to exhibit the ratios of N to Y in each single life... these logarithms being added to the logarithms of the present value of money... will give a series of numbers, the sum of which will show the value of the annuity sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For annuity and multi-life valuation use precomputed logarithmic tables of mortality ratios and sum appropriate logarithms to obtain present values — a practical computational rubric for actuarial calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of life tables: median survival and demographic implications
rubrics_metrics.description: From the same tables, it appears, that the half of those that are born are dead in 17 years time... So that, instead of murmuring... we ought with patience... to account it as a blessing that we have survived, perhaps by many years, that period of life, at which the half of the whole race of mankind does not arrive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use life-table-derived median survival to inform social and policy perspectives and temper expectations about longevity; derive policy inferences (e.g., on family formation) from demographic rates cautiously and quantitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for observing animalcules in dental/gingival gritty matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Examining a kind of gritty matter from between my teeth, and mixing it sometimes with rain-water, and sometimes with spittle, both which before had no animalcules, I then discovered with admiration a great number of very small ones moving; ... of these I discerned thousands in a drop of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect particulate matter from between teeth, suspend in clean rainwater or spittle that initially lacks animalcules, and examine a drop under microscope to detect and classify microorganisms; the medium choice affects visibility and lifeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of observed animalcules by motion and shape
rubrics_metrics.description: A second sort, much more numerous, turned themselves round like a top, and moved sometimes in a spiral manner. A third sort sometimes appeared oval, and at other times round; they moved swiftly by each other, like gnats playing in the air; and of these I discerned thousands in a drop of water; ... also a few larger ones, having a very strong and swift motion in the water, like eels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document distinct behavioral/morphological classes (e.g., eel-like swift, top-rotating spirals, many tiny oval/round forms) and quantify density per drop where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing lifeness and chemical sensitivity of micro-objects (vinegar test)
rubrics_metrics.description: I found the same after I had washed my teeth very well with vinegar, though the vinegar killed them when they were put into it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test viability by exposure to known antiseptic/acid solutions (vinegar) and observe mortality; washing samples with such chemicals may kill organisms and alter observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and interpretation of skin 'scales' — no pores in upper skin
rubrics_metrics.description: I have... shown, that there are no pores in our upper skin, but that the moisture thrust out of our body gets through between the scales, at which places there may be possibly channels for it to issue at.... All the upper part of our skin is scaly, ... they are very like those of fish, though they are without comparison smaller, and serve to the same purpose, which is, to defend the skin. These scales lay over one another as those of fish: they were five-sided, and I could plainly perceive a border or line about them. I guessed they were about 23 times broader than thick; they lay three double, for there was not above ⅓ of each visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under microscopy, interpret superficial skin structure as overlapping scales rather than porous surface; measure relative proportions and layering to support claims about moisture passage between scales rather than through pores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observations on callous skin regions: thicker scales with globules/stripes
rubrics_metrics.description: I examined some of those scales on the inside of my hand, where the skin was thickest, and found that they differed from the others only in that they were thicker, and beset with many globules and stripes; but those on the body are clearer; and as those on the body peel and fall off for nourishment, those on the inside of the hand, by reason of a great quantity of clammy matter, driven out through the skin, are fastened to one another, so as to make a callous substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare microscopic structure in different body regions to explain differences such as callous formation (thicker scales, adhesion via secreted matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-identification criterion for 'unguis odoratus' (fresh-water bivalve)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the unguis odoratus was part of a fresh water conchylium. ... The unguis odoratus, according to Dioscorides is found in the lakes of India, where nard grows; ... it is gathered after the lakes are dried up with the summer heats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textual sources describing habitat (lakes where nard grows, collected after drying) to infer that the ancient 'unguis odoratus' was a freshwater bivalve rather than a marine operculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use linguistic and taxonomic synonyms from classical sources to infer mollusk type
rubrics_metrics.description: He calls this snail conchylium, and by that general name distinguishes it from all the other sorts... the onyx is expressly reckoned by Pliny among the bivalves. For (1. 32, c. 11,) he makes all these synonimous, soleu, aulos, donax, onyxi, dactylus. And again more particularly ... he says that the dactyle are of the bivalve kind, and so denominated from their resemblance to the finger nails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference classical nomenclature and synonym lists (Dioscorides, Pliny) to map ancient names to modern taxonomic groups (e.g., onyx/dactylus → bivalves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade/geography and size arguments for plausibility of ancient trade in small opercula
rubrics_metrics.description: If it was generated in the nardiferous lakes on the river Ganges, how comes it that the same was brought from the Red Sea and Babylon? And why should the shell itself be brought so far as from the river Ganges to Greece, since the operculum was rarely a tenth part of the shell itself? Now if it was not used to be brought and exposed to sale, to what purpose to declare its virtues, or how could the experiment be made?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plausibility of historical trade/import claims by considering physical size/proportion, trade routes, and market practice — tiny opercula unlikely to be worth long-distance transport unless whole shells were traded; use such reasoning to reject misidentifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of using any sea-shells for calcination if purpose is calcination
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the whole, it is indifferent, what sort of shell we use in the shops, if it is to be calcined, provided it be a sea-shell. Nor do I find either Dioscorides or Celsus distinguish between the ostrea purpura or buccinum calcined; but they ascribe to them all the same caustic virtue; possibly some one species may have it in a higher degree...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the objective is to produce calcined shell powder with caustic properties, the precise species may be less important so long as it is a sea-shell; expect some variation in strength across species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation procedure for a Treatise of Navigation — arithmetic and mathematical foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: What arithmetic, in whole numbers and fractions, as also in decimals and logarithms, is necessary for the same? and what books are best for teaching so much of it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete navigation treatise should specify required arithmetic skills and recommend pedagogical resources for teaching them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: practical mechanical geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: What common practical mechanical geometry, performable by the scale and compass is sufficient?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include practical geometry methods using scale and compass appropriate for navigational tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: trigonometry (plane and spherical)
rubrics_metrics.description: What trigonometry, right lined and spherical, will suffice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover both plane and spherical trigonometry as needed for navigation and celestial observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: necessary knowledge of stars
rubrics_metrics.description: How many stars are to be known?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a star catalog or minimal set of stars students must recognize for navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: instruments and their construction/use at sea
rubrics_metrics.description: What instruments are best for use at sea, with the construction of them, and the manner of using them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the recommended navigational instruments, how to build them, and operational instructions for seafaring use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: full knowledge of the magnet
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole skill of the magnet, as to its directive virtues, and all the accidents which may befal it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include theory and practical considerations of magnetic compasses, including sources of error and how to correct or accommodate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: hydrography and coastal description
rubrics_metrics.description: The hydrography of the globe of the earth, the views of the coast, and the description of the under water-bottom of the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide maps, coastal views, and seabed descriptions (soundings) for practical navigation and safe passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: knowledge of winds and meteors
rubrics_metrics.description: The knowledge of winds and meteors, so far as the same is attainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize empirical knowledge of prevailing winds, weather patterns, and atmospheric phenomena relevant to navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: history and skill of all sorts of fishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The history and skill of all sorts of fishings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include practical and historical techniques for different fisheries encountered at sea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: sea medicine and surgery
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of medicine and surgery, peculiarly for the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover medical and surgical practices adapted to shipboard conditions and common maritime ailments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: admiralty law and maritime jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The common laws of the admiralty, and jurisdiction of the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain maritime legal principles, admiralty jurisdiction, and relevant laws for navigators and shipmasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: victualling and clothing for seamen
rubrics_metrics.description: The several victuallings and clothings fit for seamen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise on provisioning, rations, and suitable clothing for different climates and voyage lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: tides, currents, and eddies
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole science of ebbing and flowing, as also of currents and eddies at sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe tidal theory, current patterns, and eddy behavior with practical navigation implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: dromometry and ship motion measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Dromometry, and the measures of a ship's motion at sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present methods for measuring ship speed and distance travelled (log/measure techniques).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: shipbuilding, rigging, and use of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The building of ships of all sorts, with the several rigging and sails for each species, and the use of all the parts and motions of a ship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ship design, construction techniques, rigging plans, sail-handling, and functional explanations of ship components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: naval economy by voyage/country
rubrics_metrics.description: Naval economy, according to several voyages and countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss provisioning, crew economies, costs, and logistical practices tailored to voyage types and regional conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: rowing, canting, and sailing techniques for all vessel types
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of canting, rowing, and sailing, of all the several sorts of vessels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide maneuvering techniques (oared and sailed), handling for various hull forms, and tactical seamanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: naval ordnance and maritime armatures
rubrics_metrics.description: The gunnery, fire-works, and other armatures peculiar to sea and sea-fights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include naval artillery practice, explosive/pyrotechnic uses, and shipboard armament deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: best practices for loading/unloading commodities
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of loading and unloading the chief commodities to the best advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe stowage planning, weight distribution, and efficient cargo handling for safety and commercial efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: weighing and recovering sunken ships and goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of weighing sunken ships and goods, as also of diving for sunken goods in deep water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document salvage techniques, lifting methodologies, and diving practices for recovery of submerged vessels and cargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: materials science for naval affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The general philosophy of the motion and figures of the air, the sea, and of seasons, of timber, iron, hemp, tar, brimstone, tallow, &c. and of their several uses in naval affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze properties and uses of common naval materials and how environmental motion/seasonality affects their performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: surveys of major European navies and infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of five or six of the best navies of Europe, with that of the arsenals, magazines, docks, yards, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include comparative surveys of major fleets, shipyards, armament depots, and naval infrastructure for strategic and technical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: inventories of oceangoing shipping by state
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of all the shipping able to cross the seas belonging to each kingdom and state of Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide inventories and classifications of oceangoing merchant/military ships by polity for logistical and economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: global commercial geography and commodity flows
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of all the chief commercial parts of the world; with mention of what commodities are originally carried from, and ultimately to, any of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map major trade routes, origin-destination commodity flows, and trading specializations of regions for navigation and commerce planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: chronicle of notable sea-fights and naval expeditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of the chief sea-fights, and all other naval expeditions and exploits, relating to war, trade, or discovery, which has happened in this last century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile historical accounts of major naval engagements and voyages to inform tactics, strategy, and navigation knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: telescopes' advantageous uses at sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the most advantageous use of telescopes for several purposes at sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe practical telescope applications (navigation, lookout, signaling) and recommended designs for maritime conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: knowledge of sea depths and atmospheric heights
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the several depths of the sea, and heights of the atmospheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide empirical soundings/depth records and atmospheric pressure/height observations relevant to seamanship and navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatise content requirement: desalination and making sea-water potable
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of making sea-water fresh and potable, and fit for all uses in food and physic at sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include methods for producing potable water from seawater, storage/preservation techniques, and medical uses onboard ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical observations and methods for freshwater pearl fishing and pearl identification
rubrics_metrics.description: In the warm months... the poor people go into the water and take them up... by common estimate, not above one shell in a hundred may have a pearl... The young muscles have no pearls in them. The part where the pearl lies is in the toe or lesser end... The shells that have the best pearls are wrinkled, twisted, or bunched, and not smooth and equal as those that have none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For identifying pearl-bearing freshwater mussels, inspect shells for wrinkling/twisting, check the 'toe' region for pearls, and be aware of common small-fraction yields (approx. 1% with pearls, fewer clear). Note common pilfering practices when observing catches.
